notable_claims: Students were expelled or reprimanded for using profanity or 'rude' language in Netnews and email.
Universities banned newsgroups like rec.humor.funny and alt.sex based on content descriptions rather than specific posts.
Case Western administrators deleted a post containing source code to prevent potential network disruption.
A federal court ruled against the University of Wisconsin at Eau Claire, stating that content-based prohibitions on 'racist email' could not survive constitutional screening.
organizations: University of Wisconsin at Eau Claire
classification.summary: A comprehensive summary of censorship and disciplinary actions regarding computer use at various universities in 1991. It documents the banning of specific newsgroups, deletion of source code and images, and student punishments for 'offensive' or 'rude' electronic communications. The list highlights early conflicts between university administrative policies and First Amendment rights.
classification.title: Banned Computer Material 1991 (end of year update)

identity.subject: Banned Computer Material 1991 (end of year update)

notable_claims: Text-based newsgroups are unlikely to meet the Miller v. California obscenity test.
State universities are bound by the 14th Amendment in formulating sexual harassment policies that may impact access to information.
classification.summary: Mike Godwin of the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) challenged Iowa State University's decision to restrict access to certain Usenet newsgroups. The university had excluded groups based on potential conflicts with child protection, pornography, and sexual harassment laws. Godwin argued that text-based newsgroups generally do not meet legal definitions of obscenity or violate federal child pornography statutes.
classification.title: news policy at iowa state

notable_claims: Requiring a signed form to access controversial newsgroups may violate the American Library Association's Library Bill of Rights.
University campus mail and news systems can be viewed as 'limited public forums' subject to First Amendment standards against viewpoint-based discrimination.
The practice of segregating materials by prejudicial labels or lists is considered a tool of censorship according to ALA guidelines.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie of the EFF critiques a new Usenet access policy at Iowa State University that restricts 'controversial' newsgroups to a non-default list requiring a signed form for access. Kadie argues that treating computer networks as library resources makes such restrictions a violation of the Library Bill of Rights and First Amendment principles regarding limited public forums.
classification.title: Re: New news censorship policy at Iowa State University

identity.subject: Re: New news censorship policy at Iowa State University

notable_claims: The new censorship policy was not approved by the Comp Ctr Newsgroup committee.
The University Computation Advisory Committee did not approve the policy.
classification.summary: John Hascall urges the community to protest a new newsgroup censorship policy at Iowa State University. He claims that both the Computation Center Newsgroup committee and the University Computation Advisory Committee rejected the policy before its implementation.
classification.title: What to do about the new Newsgroup Censorship Policy at ISU

identity.subject: What to do about the new Newsgroup Censorship Policy at ISU

notable_claims: Adult-oriented newsgroups accounted for approximately 6.83% of total Usenet traffic in November 1991.
The alt.sex group had roughly 210,000 readers, representing 12.7% of all newsreaders at the time.
classification.summary: Lars P. Fischer responds to claims that Usenet is primarily used for pornography, specifically countering an article in the German version of EMMA. Using reader statistics and traffic volume data from UUNET, Fischer argues that while adult content exists, it does not constitute the majority of users or network traffic.
classification.title: Re: The USENET pornographic network

notable_claims: Removing a newsgroup is equivalent to banning a magazine from an academic library.
Stanford University banned rec.humor.funny in 1989 but lifted the ban after a committee recommended following library policy.
The University of Waterloo banned rec.humor.funny and alt.sex, lifting the ban in October 1991.
classification.summary: In response to a student's inquiry about Usenet censorship at Iowa State University, Carl Kadie provides resources from the EFF archive. He argues that university newsgroup selection should follow established library principles of intellectual freedom and professional selection policies. The post references previous successful challenges to newsgroup bans at Stanford University and the University of Waterloo.
classification.title: Re: New news censorship policy at Iowa State University

identity.subject: Re: New news censorship policy at Iowa State University

notable_claims: Screening Netnews for offensive articles may increase a university's legal liability.
Courts have historically found institutions free from liability when control of publications remains with students rather than administrators.
The Cubby v. CompuServe decision suggests that distributors without editorial control are not liable for defamatory statements.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to a query about university liability for offensive Netnews content by citing EFF resources and legal precedents. He argues that exercising editorial control or screening may actually increase a university's legal liability compared to a no-screening policy. The post emphasizes the distinction between institutional administration and student editorial functions.
classification.title: Re: Inappropriate Use by 2714sviatkos

notable_claims: University computer use policies should not override contractual guarantees of freedom from institutional censorship.
Students should be free to express opinions publicly and privately per the Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to a notice from Marquette University regarding the suspension of a student's computer access due to an 'inflammatory message.' Kadie argues that punishing students for speech in a free forum violates academic freedom and contractual guarantees against institutional censorship. He cites the Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students to support his position.
classification.title: Re: Inappropriate Use by 2714sviatkos

notable_claims: Iowa State University's policy prohibiting 'rude' material likely infringes on Constitutionally-protected rights.
Federal district courts in UWM POST v. U. of Wisconsin and Doe v. U. of Michigan struck down campus speech codes as First Amendment violations.
The UWM Post decision specifically involved email communication.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie challenges Iowa State University's policy prohibiting 'rude' material on university computing facilities. He argues that government-enforced courtesy violates First Amendment protections and cites legal precedents against campus speech codes. The discussion highlights the tension between institutional guidelines for electronic communication and constitutional free speech rights.
classification.title: Re: BS!

notable_claims: Academic environments should prioritize the free flow of information over individual privacy to increase productivity.
Restricting system visibility (like 'ps') hinders the ability of users to help one another resolve technical issues without waiting for administrators.
classification.summary: Eric Lee Green argues against restricting the Unix 'ps' command, citing a case where monitoring processes helped identify a user accidentally exhausting swap space with multiple MIT C-Scheme instances. He contends that in academic environments, the free flow of system information promotes productivity and cross-pollination over individual privacy. He suggests that while corporate settings may require privacy, university systems benefit from transparency to allow peer-to-peer assistance.
classification.title: Re: System Accounting: Fascist Tool?

notable_claims: Privacy is a right regardless of whether an individual has something to hide.
Contents of academic computers are private by default unless the owner chooses to make them public.
Faculty have a right to keep research on academic computers private until it is polished and ready for publication.
classification.summary: Dean Gottehrer argues against the notion that privacy is only for those with something to hide, comparing it to Fifth Amendment rights. He asserts that contents of academic computers should remain private unless explicitly made public by the creator. This includes research in progress and files belonging to students and staff.
classification.title: Positivism, privacy, and the flow of information

identity.subject: Re: Positivism, privacy, and the flow of information

notable_claims: MUD traffic accounted for 30% of total network usage during a weekend period.
Interactive response time on 56KB connections was insufficient for real-time MUD battles.
classification.summary: Brick Verser provides network traffic statistics from K-State to analyze the impact of Multi-User Dungeon (MUD) gaming on campus bandwidth. The data shows that despite policies prohibiting MUD play during school hours, it remained a top application by volume. The author notes that while T1 connections handle this traffic easily, 56KB connections suffered from latency issues affecting gameplay.
classification.title: Network utilization by MUD players

identity.subject: Network utilization by MUD players (was Re: Gaming)
